newsitem.title: GREECE: OLYMPICS-ATHENS BID ORGANISERS APPEAL TO REALITY.
newsitem.headline: OLYMPICS-ATHENS BID ORGANISERS APPEAL TO REALITY.

text.p: Athens bid organisers, chastened by Greece's failure to win the 1996 Olympics, have substituted reality for rhetoric in their fight to host the 2004 Games.
Greece, which hosted the first Olympics of the modern era in 1896, was the sentimental favourite to stage the 1996 centenary Games.
But the International Olympic Comittee, concerned that Athens might not meet the demands of a giants sports festival decided to award the Games instead to Atlanta.
Now the Greeks are determined to get it right.
"This is a totally new bid with a totally new attitude," said bidding committee head Yanna Angelopoulos. "Eighty percent of the sports facilities are in place and we have the money for the rest.
"We are proud of our Olympic heritage but we don't depend on it to win the Games. The view that we are owed the Olympics and statements that we would never bid again were wrong."
Angelopoulos, wife of steel works and shipping tycoon Theodore Angelopoulos, was picked last year by Prime Minister Costas Simitis to head the new Athens effort.

The elegant 41-year-old lawyer is also the major underwriter of the bid and has put much effort into mending relations with the IOC, angered by what was perceived as Greece's arrogant approach to the 1996 bid.

"Mrs Angelopoulos is certainly a positive change for Athens but many other things must also improve. Greece has good sports facilities but is a country plagued by strikes, pollution economic problems, and lack of organisation," one IOC member said.

Athens's assets include an 80,000-seat Olympic stadium and two indoor stadiums, while a new $2.5 billion airport and a $2.1 billion subway system, which were supposed to be operational last year, are scheduled to be completed by 2001.

"I can assure you that these works will be completed in time regardless of the Olympics," Angelopoulos said. "The metro will drastically reduce pollution. Athens is changing and we feel more ready than ever to host the Olympics."

The bid committee has said more than 90 percent of Athens' four million inhabitants back the effort to bring the Games home but groups such as Greenpeace have warned of serious damage to the environment from large-scale Games-related construction.
Another concern is money. The bidding dossier says Greece will spend some $1.6 billion if Athens wins the Games and expects a profit of $36.6 million.

But budgets in Greece are rarely met. Officials said this month that the Athens' world athletics championships in August, originally forecast to have a balanced budget, will now post a $14 million loss.

"The cost of new sports facilities along with other works will be two or three times more than budgeted. If we get the Olympics we will be paying them for years," said sports analyst Phillipos Syrigos, projecting a deficit of more than $5 billion.

Greeks are already hard pressed to meet the requirements of the European Monetary Union by the year 2000 and the government abolished this year a series of tax breaks which will yield some $1.8 billion to finance towering state debts.

The government also plans to spend some $14 billion in the next four years for buying new weapons to counter perceived threats by rival Turkey and Simitis has said he may resort to foreign borrowing to come up with the sum.
Another problem is hotel space. Athens has a capacity of 25,000 rooms while it expects 34,000 officials and 100,000 visitors.
It plans to use hotels outside Athens, camping sites and even cruise ships to put them up if it wins the Games.

"Athens has the advantage of hosting the world athletics championships, the biggest sports event of 1997, one month before the IOC votes for the host city. If it does well, it will be a very strong candidate," the IOC official said.
